title_en: In ‘You Can See Everything,’ Elizabeth Holmes meets her equal in comedian Nathan Fielder
title_fa: In ‘You Can See Everything,’ Elizabeth Holmes meets her equal in comedian Nathan Fielder
excerpt_en: Nathan Fielder's documentary about disgraced Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes has created a constellation of colliding personas that interrogate the very nature of authenticity.
excerpt_fa: Nathan Fielder's documentary about disgraced Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes has created a constellation of colliding personas that interrogate the very nature of authenticity.
content_en:
“Isn’t it weird that I, like, did a TV show about kind of a business scam, and you got in trouble for like … a business scam?” comedian and filmmaker Nathan Fielder gently asks Elizabeth Holmes.
One month before the notorious Theranos CEO surrendered to begin her 11-year criminal fraud sentence in 2023, Holmes and her husband contacted A24 as a last-ditch effort to exonerate her in the public eye, suggesting they send a film crew to document her final days of freedom. Alongside director Lance Oppenheim, Fielder — a cringe-comedy mastermind whose work often walks the line between fact and fiction — embraced the impossible project of figuring out who the infamous Stanford dropout really is.
“I never actually made that connection,” says Holmes. “I think it’s a pretty different situation.”
No one is better prepared than Fielder to probe the depths of Holmes’ psyche. His satirical docu-reality show “Nathan for You” catapulted him to cult stardom as he assumed the role of an exaggerated, deadpan version of himself who tries to help struggling small businesses by executing asinine interventions. In one early episode that went viral, Fielder convinces a coffee shop to change its name to “Dumb Starbucks” as a marketing stunt, but consults a lawyer to help him toe the flimsy line of parody law and escape legal trouble.
“If you just said that, you know, Theranos was a comedy bit, maybe you could get off scot-free,” Fielder says to Holmes.
“It was real.”
“I was just kind of making a little joke. Maybe it was in bad taste.”
We already know that Elizabeth Holmes is not innocent. What we still can’t figure out, though, is whether she really, truly believes she did nothing wrong. Even as she sat on trial — listening to testimonies from investors who lost hundreds of millions of dollars, whistleblowers who were silenced when they flagged that Theranos’ blood-testing devices didn’t work, and patients who acted on incorrect blood test results — Holmes never wavered.
Across Fielder’s body of metatextual comedy, even his most reverent fans can’t quite figure out when he’s acting, when he’s being himself, and if Fielder himself even knows where to draw that line anymore.
In that way, Fielder is just like Holmes: After over a decade in the public eye, onlookers remain captivated by each of their ambiguous personas.
“The world believes a reality about me that isn’t true,” she tells Fielder. “I know I didn’t commit any crime.”
[The rest of this review contains spoilers.]
Early on in filming, The New York Times had just published a profile of Holmes, which was widely criticized at the time for allowing Holmes to portray herself as an innocent mom deprived of the chance to watch her kids grow up.
And yet, Holmes and her husband, hotel heir Billy Evans, were livid about the article.
At one point in an interview, Holmes tells the Times reporter that she wasn’t offended by actress Amanda Seyfried’s portrayal of her in Hulu’s miniseries “The Dropout” because “they’re not playing me. They’re playing a character I created.”
She and her husband insist that the quote was taken out of context. They claim that they have evidence that Holmes actually said, “They’re playing a character they created,” relieving her from any implication that she admitted to concocting an inauthentic persona as CEO of Theranos.
Fielder asks Evans multiple times to share this evidence so he can prove that Holmes was misquoted. He never does.
Once Holmes reports to prison, Fielder is agonized as he tries to make something out of his month of footage. He calls in the perfect sidekick to help him dissect her confounding behavior: the very actress who portrays her in “The Dropout.”
Fielder plays Seyfried a brutal clip from his time with Holmes, when he tries watching “The Dropout” with the subject of the series. When they get to a tense scene involving Holmes’ manipulative ex-boyfriend and former Theranos partner in crime Sunny Balwani — who is also now in prison — Holmes can no longer bear to watch this fictional version of herself. She turns away and cries.
In other words, Seyfried is watching Holmes react to Seyfried’s portrayal of Holmes, who was probably also playing a character herself. But Seyfried is not the only one creating a crude approximation of the real Elizabeth. Evans has constructed a lifelike AI avatar of his wife, trapped inside of a large vertical screen that he wheels over to the dinner table to sit with him and his kids as though she’s actually there.
The remainder of the film is a constellation of colliding personas. Though it’s a nonfiction documentary, it’s clear that everyone involved is, to some extent, also performing for the cameras. How could they not? Seyfried’s determination to understand Holmes’ story seems pure, but it’s not lost on the audience that she just scored a significant role in one of the most talked-about movies of the year.
Meanwhile, Evans behaves in such an unfathomably egregious manner that he may even be intentionally playing the villain to drum up sympathy for his reviled wife.
Evans knows that Fielder and Oppenheim are not convinced of Holmes’ innocence. This documentary will not sway anyone to believe that his wife is being wrongly held in federal custody. But Evans makes himself appear so appallingly unlikable that some viewers may leave the theater feeling bad for Holmes, seeing her as a victim and allowing her to double down on another persona she adopted while on trial: a harmless, docile woman who was manipulated by her ex-partner to obliviously tell a cascade of increasingly harmful lies.
Once Holmes is in jail, Fielder is not allowed to bring recording devices when he visits her, so he tries to write a script of their conversations from memory, struggling to accurately re-create the nuances of a conversation where every last word carries immense meaning. With Seyfried reprising her role from “The Dropout,” we see the pair practice reading the script, editing the language as Fielder tries to...

content_en:
It’s been a couple of days since Apple’s big smart home announcement, and we have some more information — and a bunch of new questions — about the Apple HomeView. The device has plenty of computing oomph, is always connected to power, and looks like a perfect place to run a bunch of apps. And yet the HomeView is relying almost entirely on CarPlay. What gives here?
Apple’s HomeView has an app problem
On The Vergecast: Relying on CarPlay, slinking back to X, competing with Muse, and much more.
On The Vergecast: Relying on CarPlay, slinking back to X, competing with Muse, and much more.
On this episode of The Vergecast, David and Nilay try to make sense of the HomeView’s app situation, and why Apple would choose not to make its home hub into its own app platform. After that, they talk about the latest Gemini model and whether building the best model matters if you can’t build the best products around it. They then debate the merits of returning to X, why none of the supposed Twitter replacements worked, the latest in Brendan Carr nonsense, and much more.

title_en: Jev is Vercel’s fastest-adopted AI model ever
title_fa: Jev is Vercel’s fastest-adopted AI model ever
excerpt_en: The data comes from Vercel's AI gateway, a unified API service similar to OpenRouter.
excerpt_fa: The data comes from Vercel's AI gateway, a unified API service similar to OpenRouter.
content_en:
Jev has become the fastest adopted AI model ever — at least by some measures.
Vercel data published on Thursday shows that, within two weeks of its launch, the buzzy decision model was being used by 35% of paid teams, with nearly double the reach of the second most popular model, Sonnet 5.5. It’s the fastest adoption a model has ever seen in its first two weeks, according to Vercel’s data, and a major accomplishment for the model’s creators, TypeSafe AI.
Published in limited release on September 15, Jev is designed as a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs. Limiting the outputs lets the model run cheaper and faster than alternatives like Sonnet, making it ideal for classifying large quantities of data quickly. That new approach has attracted significant buzz in the weeks since Jev’s release — inspiring competing offerings from OpenAI and Amazon, among others — but until now there has been little hard data to back up the good vibes.
The data comes from Vercel’s AI gateway, a unified API service similar to OpenRouter. It’s a necessarily limited view — particularly at risk of undercounting major labs like OpenAI and Anthropic that offer their own APIs — but it shows the buzz around Jev really did translate into actual usage. In fact, Vercel was an early adopter of Jev, using it to replace GPT-6 Luna for classifying harmful commands.
The report also shows continuing momentum for open source models, which now account for more than 70% of the tokens processed through Vercel’s gateway and nearly 25% of the total spend.
While open source models are capturing a larger share of the market, the market is also growing fast. Spending on frontier labs has grown tenfold, even as it accounts for a smaller share of overall spend, giving credence to the idea that frontier models and open source alternatives may turn out to be complementary rather than competitive.

title_en: Analogue is re-releasing its SNES and Genesis consoles with some nice upgrades
title_fa: Analogue is re-releasing its SNES and Genesis consoles with some nice upgrades
excerpt_en: Analogue announced new versions of its Super Nt and Mega Sg retro consoles today with a "reworked industrial design" and built-in wireless connectivity for controllers and accessories. Like the original versions, the new Super Nt Plus and Mega Sg Plus are able to play Nintendo...
excerpt_fa: Analogue announced new versions of its Super Nt and Mega Sg retro consoles today with a "reworked industrial design" and built-in wireless connectivity for controllers and accessories. Like the original versions, the new Super Nt Plus and Mega Sg Plus are able to play Nintendo...
content_en:
Analogue announced new versions of its Super Nt and Mega Sg retro consoles today with a “reworked industrial design” and built-in wireless connectivity for controllers and accessories. Like the original versions, the new Super Nt Plus and Mega Sg Plus are able to play Nintendo and Sega Genesis cartridges using an FPGA processor that perfectly recreates the functionality of Nintendo and Sega’s 16-bit consoles without the need for emulation.
Analogue is re-releasing its SNES and Genesis consoles with some nice upgrades
The Super Nt Plus and Mega Sg Plus add USB-C and USB-A ports plus built-in wireless connections for controllers.
The Super Nt Plus and Mega Sg Plus add USB-C and USB-A ports plus built-in wireless connections for controllers.
Although neither of the new consoles allows SNES or Genesis titles to be played in 4K like the Analogue 3D does with Nintendo 64 titles, the 1080p Super Nt and Mega Sg Plus add a USB-C port so you can power them with the cables you already use with your phone and mobile devices, and an additional USB-A port for other peripherals. Both consoles also introduce a built-in Bluetooth or a low-latency 2.4Ghz wireless connection for connecting to gamepads without requiring an additional controller port dongle.
Wired controllers are still an option, and the upgraded consoles can both be powered up remotely using whatever gamepad is connected as the primary controller. Analogue also says game cartridges can now be hot swapped without having to completely power down either console after quitting the game through a menu.
Both the Super Nt Plus and Mega Sg Plus will be available for preorder starting on October 19th at 9AM PT/11AM ET for $219.99 with shipping expected to start sometime in December, later this year.

title_en: A fake WhatsApp clone is showing up before the real version on the Play Store
title_fa: A fake WhatsApp clone is showing up before the real version on the Play Store
excerpt_en: After a Chrome clone was spotted on the Play Store earlier this week, a user on Reddit says they're seeing a fake version of WhatsApp in a "sponsored" slot above the real version. As reported earlier by Android Authority, the WhatsApp dupe has racked up over 500,000 downloads...
excerpt_fa: After a Chrome clone was spotted on the Play Store earlier this week, a user on Reddit says they're seeing a fake version of WhatsApp in a "sponsored" slot above the real version. As reported earlier by Android Authority, the WhatsApp dupe has racked up over 500,000 downloads...
content_en:
After a Chrome clone was spotted on the Play Store earlier this week, a user on Reddit says they’re seeing a fake version of WhatsApp in a “sponsored” slot above the real version. As reported earlier by Android Authority, the WhatsApp dupe has racked up over 500,000 downloads and, at the time of writing, its Play Store listing is still live.
A fake WhatsApp clone is showing up before the real version on the Play Store
The ‘WhatsApp Messenger’ dupe reportedly popped up as a sponsored result above the real version.
The ‘WhatsApp Messenger’ dupe reportedly popped up as a sponsored result above the real version.
Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The WhatsApp clone is from a developer going by “Agment Assets sallu” who doesn’t currently have anything else listed on the Play Store. Their listing for the WhatsApp impostor has the same icon, screenshots, and text as the real version, but the real WhatsApp has over 10 billion downloads, an “editor’s choice” badge, and over 246 million reviews. Android Authority points out that the WhatsApp clone may be using Google Play’s Early Access program to disable public user reviews, which could have helped users warn people against downloading the app.

title_en: A week with RTX Spark: everything we’ve learned using Nvidia’s new laptops
title_fa: A week with RTX Spark: everything we’ve learned using Nvidia’s new laptops
excerpt_en: Nvidia's RTX Spark N1X processor is finally here, and we've been collectively testing a small fortune's worth of powerful laptops sporting this new "superchip." RTX Spark is designed to be a high-performing Arm-based SoC for laptops and small desktop computers, rivaling the best...
excerpt_fa: Nvidia's RTX Spark N1X processor is finally here, and we've been collectively testing a small fortune's worth of powerful laptops sporting this new "superchip." RTX Spark is designed to be a high-performing Arm-based SoC for laptops and small desktop computers, rivaling the best...
content_en:
Nvidia’s RTX Spark N1X processor is finally here, and we’ve been collectively testing a small fortune’s worth of powerful laptops sporting this new “superchip.” RTX Spark is designed to be a high-performing Arm-based SoC for laptops and small desktop computers, rivaling the best from Apple, Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm. It has loads of cores, Nvidia RTX Blackwell graphics, and enough power and unified memory to run sizable local AI models.
A week with RTX Spark: everything we’ve learned using Nvidia’s new laptops
Nvidia’s new Arm-based laptop chip is an exciting new challenger, but exclusively for the high-end.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
The flagship placement is inside Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra with a staggering 128GB of unified memory, which our own Tom Warren fully reviewed. Sean Hollister has been testing a 64GB version of the Asus ProArt P16, which I’ve also been testing in its top-spec 128GB config. Since I’m the most spoiled of the lot, I also have a 64GB Lenovo Yoga 9n 2-in-1 and a 32GB HP OmniBook Ultra in for testing.
All of these laptops have the same N1X chip with 20 CPU cores and 6,144 GPU CUDA cores, and they’re all wildly expensive — ranging from the HP OmniBook at $3,199.99 to the Asus ProArt’s $6,999.99. There’s an 18-core / 5,120 CUDA N1X chip in lower cost configs, but that only gets as cheap as $2,599.99 for a Surface Laptop Ultra or a smaller Asus ProArt P14 with 24GB of RAM.
These are big and expensive laptops built on new chips. They’re meant for developers, coders, and content creators who might also want the ability to use local AI and even play games using the latest Nvidia tech like DLSS 5. There’s a lot to test, and we have not had a ton of time to test it all. So below you won’t find an exhaustive scored review of any one laptop, but instead our impressions and thoughts from three writers using five laptops for a week.
Is Nvidia’s “superchip” really all that super? Are Apple, Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm officially on notice? Have any of us gotten any sleep?
Does it just work?
Antonio Di Benedetto: Windows on Arm is no longer a wholly subpar experience like it was a few years ago. Thanks in large part to the push around Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X chips, lots of development has been put into native Arm-based apps for Windows. And many x86 apps work fine via Microsoft’s Prism emulation layer.
Adobe has had native Arm versions of Photoshop and Premiere for some time now, and even though my precious Lightroom Classic is still an x86-based app I don’t notice any issues using it on Arm. At this point, you’ve gotta be relying on specialized software that’s exclusively x86 based for Windows on Arm to be a non-starter — or you want to freely play any games out there without any worry of incompatibilities.
Sean Hollister: Every so often, there’s that moment when an app takes longer to load than it should, and I wonder whether it’ll load at all. Even then, it typically loads. Occasionally, it takes more than one try. My Evernote notes disappeared a few times one day when I alt-tabbed away, but a force refresh fixed that. And apps don’t seem to respect my system preference for dark mode.
But I largely agree with Antonio. title_en: Mark Wahlberg on using AI in film ‘the right way’ and being open to an AI clone carrying on his legacy
title_fa: Mark Wahlberg on using AI in film ‘the right way’ and being open to an AI clone carrying on his legacy
excerpt_en: Actor and angel investor Mark Wahlberg says he's OK with using AI in filmmaking, provided it's used "to enhance what you're doing."
excerpt_fa: Actor and angel investor Mark Wahlberg says he's OK with using AI in filmmaking, provided it's used "to enhance what you're doing."
content_en:
Even as Hollywood remains divided over the use of AI in filmmaking, actor and director Mark Wahlberg believes the technology has a place in the industry as long as it’s used the right way.
Wahlberg, who’s also an entrepreneur and angel investor, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt to share his perspective on AI’s role in filmmaking, and how he’s open to having an AI likeness of himself carry on his legacy.
The actor said he plans to potentially use AI to enhance certain aspects of the upcoming Pete Rose biopic, in which he’ll star in the title role.
“It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors. But if you can use it to enhance what you’re doing, I’m all for that.”
That said, Wahlberg made special mention of his belief that storytelling should remain at the heart of filmmaking.
“I’ve done big, effects-driven movies,” Wahlberg said. “I think I was in that kind of sweet spot when the first Jurassic Park was made, or when Perfect Storm came out, and you had that wave, the 100-foot wave that was in the trailer. Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images. Now, I think it’s hard to do that, so I’m not so passionate about effects-driven movies per se, as opposed to real storytelling.”
When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault, a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea.
“I would be interested because I think in the future, if that’s where things go, it would be cool that my children or my grandchildren could be in charge of my likeness and my image, and hopefully put me in some good movies,” Wahlberg said. “It’ll be interesting to see where things go.”
He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness.
“I think it’s cool if I’m no longer able to do it or don’t exist, and if it could continue and people want to see it, I think it’d be interesting to see where things go,” Wahlberg said. “I think there’s certain things from my childhood that I wish still existed and were still a part of my life […] I wouldn’t be opposed to it. I think people are going to have massive opportunities to watch whatever it is they want, and if there’s a real audience for that, they should be entitled to have what they want to see.”

title_en: MapQuest will now show you where Flock cameras are in your neighborhood
title_fa: MapQuest will now show you where Flock cameras are in your neighborhood
excerpt_en: You can see the locations of known outdoor surveillance cameras in the MapQuest app.
excerpt_fa: You can see the locations of known outdoor surveillance cameras in the MapQuest app.
content_en:
MapQuest will now show you where Flock cameras are in your neighborhood
You can see the locations of known outdoor surveillance cameras in the app.
MapQuest has been on quite the unexpected tear over the last couple of months. The mapping service's app surged in popularity after it refused to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America (unlike Google Maps and Apple Maps). MapQuest also added useful, long-overdue features like Android Auto support and public transit directions.
The app now has another handy tool. You can toggle a layer that shows known outdoor surveillance cameras and license plate readers.
The layer will show you where Flock cameras are. It also displays the locations of cameras from the likes of Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia and Verkada. The layer sits alongside options to view traffic and incidents, so it should be easy to find in the app.
MapQuest announced the update with a short video that's set to Rockwell's "Somebody's Watching Me." Chef's kiss, no notes.
You might not be able to easily avoid these cameras on your commute or other usual routes, but the layer may be helpful in illustrating how pervasive these things are in your area. It's useful information to have for those who are trying to rid their neighborhoods of surveillance cams.

title_en: Veritas expands its anti-counterfeit chip to jewelry, trophies, and fragrance bottles
title_fa: Veritas expands its anti-counterfeit chip to jewelry, trophies, and fragrance bottles
excerpt_en: Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands' marks and passing off dupes, known as "superfakes," as genuine items. A startup called Veritas wants to tackle the problem with its own chip that verifies goods.
excerpt_fa: Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands' marks and passing off dupes, known as "superfakes," as genuine items. A startup called Veritas wants to tackle the problem with its own chip that verifies goods.
content_en:
Counterfeits of luxury goods are a major problem for fashion houses. Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands’ marks and passing off dupes, known as “superfakes,” as genuine items. A startup called Veritas wants to tackle the problem with its own chip that verifies goods.
Veritas was founded by Luci Holland, a former Tesla technical product manager who also has a background in design and art. Its chip is built to be easily inserted into products without damaging them. Brands can use it to verify whether a product is the real deal, and customers can show a certificate of ownership through the company’s app.
Holland said other approaches are easier to defeat, because a digital record can be reproduced through a copied QR code or static NFC link.
“Our approach combines secure, authenticated chip responses with integration into the product itself. Our chip generates a secure response with each tap and includes a tamper-detection wire. We make the connection between the object and its digital identity part of the proof,” Holland said.
The Veritas founder told TechCrunch over email that the company has just introduced the second version of its chip, which works on metal surfaces and can be scanned through glass.
“The next-generation chip is ready for production and supports a broader range of applications, including jewelry, trophies, hard-surface products, and glass objects such as fragrance bottles,” Holland said. “Alongside our garment integrations, this gives brands more ways to incorporate authentication directly into their products.”
This week, the startup announced a partnership with ATHLOS, a women’s track-and-field competition founded by Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian, who is also an investor in Veritas. As part of the partnership, all 18 championship crowns will include Veritas’ chips so they can be verified.
The company also embedded a chip into a pair of LeBron James’ first Nike shoes, reimagined by artist Adam Port. Tapping a phone to the shoe brings up its history and story.
The company has so far raised $1.75 million in pre-seed funding led by Ohanian’s venture firm Seven Seven Six, with participation from DoorDash co-founder Stanley Tang; Gloria Zhu, co-founder of skincare brand Reys; and former TechCrunch editor Josh Constine.
Since its February fundraise, the company has shipped an iOS app for consumers and a brand portal that lets companies manage product records and build owner experiences. Through the app and the portal, brands can offer experiences such as clubs, event check-ins, and segmented early access to product drops.
Veritas competed in this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield, which ran Tuesday through Thursday. A winner was announced Thursday afternoon.

title_en: Technics EAH-A1000 review: Superior sound and excellent ANC in a premium package
title_fa: Technics EAH-A1000 review: Superior sound and excellent ANC in a premium package
excerpt_en: Technics' flagship over-ear wireless headphones are light on compromises, but enter a competitive market.
excerpt_fa: Technics' flagship over-ear wireless headphones are light on compromises, but enter a competitive market.
content_en:
Technics EAH-A1000 review: Superior sound and excellent ANC in a premium package
The company's flagship over-ear wireless headphones are light on compromises, but enter a competitive market.
When Technics announced the EAH-A1000 over-ear Bluetooth headphones, everything seemed fairly ordinary. Another set of premium cans entering an already crowded category. Sure, they have a few standout features on the spec sheet — magnetic fluid drivers and three-device multipoint Bluetooth, for example. At $450, they are directly taking on Sony's popular WH-1000XM6, and almost enter the same territory as Sennheiser's audiophile-friendly HDB 630.
It's a confident move from Technics, to place its flag in the lucrative, but risky, territory between high-end consumer and "affordable" specialist headphones. I've had the A1000 on the testing bench (a.k.a. my head) for a couple of weeks and my initial assessment of how "ordinary" they are might have been a little hasty.
What's new on the Technics EAH-A1000?
The feature Technics is making the most noise about is the "Magnetic Fluid" technology, but it's not new to the A1000. The AZ100 true wireless earbuds also use it, but these are the first over-ears from Technics to include it. The idea is that it reduces unwanted vibrations in the driver, in turn reducing distortion.
One other feature that stands out is the three-device multipoint Bluetooth. Seamless connection with your phone and PC can now include one more device, like a gaming console or TV. There is a slight limitation here: If you listen via LDAC (which the A1000 also supports), that will limit you to two devices maximum.
Of course there's adaptive active noise cancellation (ANC) coupled with a beamforming microphone for clearer phone calls. Other features you'd expect at this price point, such as Dolby Atmos with headtracking, wear detection, EQ/app control, a healthy 45-hour battery life (with ANC on) and lossless playback via USB-C and 3.5mm cables (both provided) are all present and correct. Cosmetically, the A1000 offers smooth lines and a stylish, but understated, design. They could pass for a Sony or Bose model at a glance.
Audio and ANC performance
Headphone marketing materials are like gourmet menus: There are a lot of decorative adjectives to describe beef. Or, in the case of headphones, 40mm drivers. I can't put my hand on my heart and say that the magnetic fluid technology Technics mentions is making a difference, but I was immediately impressed when I first put the A1000 on and pressed play on Spotify.
My music tastes skew electronic, so bass really matters. On the A1000, the low frequencies are some of the tightest I've heard. That's the best word I can find for it. The bass is present, I can feel it, but it's not vibrating in my eardrums at all. It sounds like it's firmly attached to the song with glue, in a good way. Kick drums in dance music offer a gentle thwack, in turn providing a good sense of space and dynamic range in the mix.
Pop and rock genres do a good job at exposing the mid and high frequencies. BTS' Dynamite, for example, sounds much more robust and balanced in the A1000 than it does in my car on the school run when I'm trying to animate the kids. I even heard parts of the bassline I barely knew existed. If there's a minor criticism, it's at the higher end. Listening to AC/DC or the Arctic Monkeys, the guitars sound authentic, but my ears wanted a teeny-tiny bit more sizzle out of them.
I regularly use the Sennheiser HDB 630 and the Technics A1000 surprised me with a slightly bigger sense of space and soundstage. The tight balance and well-rounded bass make them one of the strongest pairs I've tried for a long time.
The stellar sound wasn't the first thing I noticed when I put them on, the adaptive ANC is also extremely good. I'm a little fussy with noise cancellation; it's a feature I appreciate but I prefer good audio chops over superior ANC if I have to choose. With the A1000, that's not really an issue. The noise cancellation is effective for both steady sounds like fans, yet it's adaptive enough that I can't hear people talking when my spouse has guests and I'm working. I prefer it to the ANC on the HDB 630 and I'd say it's good enough to be in the same room with Sony and Bose.
App and controls
I have a folder on my phone that's a graveyard of unused headphone apps. Technics Connect hasn't made it there, yet. As control apps go, it's easy to navigate and you'll find extra settings like choosing between LDAC compatible multipoint Bluetooth (remember: max two connections) or even turning it off. There's the aforementioned EQ section, the option to choose how long before the headphones auto-turn off and a toggle to disable wear detection, among other fine helpful tools.
A note on the multipoint feature: I've never really had a good experience with it on any headphones, with my Mac usually connecting via the hands-free profile. That was my experience with the A1000, too. Even switching between my phone and my Windows laptop was unreliable. I can't confidently blame these headphones, but I didn't have much luck with two devices, let alone three.
There are no touch controls on the A1000, instead you get two buttons and a clickable volume rocker. Despite everything being on the right earcup, it doesn't feel cramped. The volume rocker is easy to find, but you click "back" for volume up, which feels counter intuitive to me. Media controls are navigated by multiple clicks on the same rocker. It's practical and works, but sometimes the button lightly sticks, turning three clicks into two, which is the difference between a skip forward and skip back.
The competition
The $449 pits the A1000 directly against Sony's WH-1000XM6, and I do think it competes well on sound quality and ANC. The choice will come down to secondary details like design and battery life and app features, with the latter being where Sony really stacks the deck. I'll come right out and say that I personally...

Pop and rock genres do a good job at exposing the mid and high frequencies. BTS' Dynamite, for example, sounds much more robust and balanced in the A1000 than it does in my car on the school run when I'm trying to animate the kids. I even heard parts of the bassline I barely knew existed. If there's a minor criticism, it's at the higher end. Listening to AC/DC or the Arctic Monkeys, the guitars sound authentic, but my ears wanted a teeny-tiny bit more sizzle out of them.
I regularly use the Sennheiser HDB 630 and the Technics A1000 surprised me with a slightly bigger sense of space and soundstage. The tight balance and well-rounded bass make them one of the strongest pairs I've tried for a long time.
The stellar sound wasn't the first thing I noticed when I put them on, the adaptive ANC is also extremely good. I'm a little fussy with noise cancellation; it's a feature I appreciate but I prefer good audio chops over superior ANC if I have to choose. With the A1000, that's not really an issue. The noise cancellation is effective for both steady sounds like fans, yet it's adaptive enough that I can't hear people talking when my spouse has guests and I'm working. I prefer it to the ANC on the HDB 630 and I'd say it's good enough to be in the same room with Sony and Bose.
App and controls
I have a folder on my phone that's a graveyard of unused headphone apps. Technics Connect hasn't made it there, yet. As control apps go, it's easy to navigate and you'll find extra settings like choosing between LDAC compatible multipoint Bluetooth (remember: max two connections) or even turning it off. There's the aforementioned EQ section, the option to choose how long before the headphones auto-turn off and a toggle to disable wear detection, among other fine helpful tools.
A note on the multipoint feature: I've never really had a good experience with it on any headphones, with my Mac usually connecting via the hands-free profile. That was my experience with the A1000, too. Even switching between my phone and my Windows laptop was unreliable. I can't confidently blame these headphones, but I didn't have much luck with two devices, let alone three.
There are no touch controls on the A1000, instead you get two buttons and a clickable volume rocker. Despite everything being on the right earcup, it doesn't feel cramped. The volume rocker is easy to find, but you click "back" for volume up, which feels counter intuitive to me. Media controls are navigated by multiple clicks on the same rocker. It's practical and works, but sometimes the button lightly sticks, turning three clicks into two, which is the difference between a skip forward and skip back.
The competition
The $449 pits the A1000 directly against Sony's WH-1000XM6, and I do think it competes well on sound quality and ANC. The choice will come down to secondary details like design and battery life and app features, with the latter being where Sony really stacks the deck. I'll come right out and say that I personally...

title_en: Replit’s CEO says the future of work is the ‘self-driving company’
title_fa: Replit’s CEO says the future of work is the ‘self-driving company’
excerpt_en: Replit CEO Amjad Masad envisions a future of “self-driving companies,” where AI agents handle day-to-day tasks and people focus on higher-level decisions.
excerpt_fa: Replit CEO Amjad Masad envisions a future of “self-driving companies,” where AI agents handle day-to-day tasks and people focus on higher-level decisions.
content_en:
Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad has seen how AI is impacting the workplace firsthand, with businesses adopting his company’s AI coding tools to develop and launch their own software. At TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, Masad shared what Replit has learned about what that means for the future of work in the AI age, including how humans will still play key roles as AI agents come to work alongside them.
He described his vision of a “self-driving company,” referring not to robotaxi makers, but how agents will come to do much of the grunt work at companies while people become more valued for their judgment and taste.
“The reality is, all of our jobs — perhaps everyone in this audience, especially — changed over the past year,” he said, addressing the audience at Disrupt. “But a big part of America and the world, they still don’t know that that change is coming, and it’s going to be surprising to a lot of people,” Masad said.
He said Replit’s team had been reflecting on how AI technology impacted their own workplace over the past year, particularly after AI agents became more reliable sometime earlier this year.
“Our company entirely changed how we operate, and I would say the closest analogy is a ‘self-driving company’,” Masad said. “The company is sort of self-improving, so a lot of the work that’s going on is driven by agents.”
Illustrating the shift, Masad said that when support tickets come in at Replit, they’re first examined by an agent, which performs the initial triaging by looking at GitHub issues, the codebase, and Linear tickets. By the time the support request reaches a person, they have all the additional information that helps them decide how best to proceed.
And when that support person decides to submit a patch to apply a fix, it’s just a click to deploy another agent.
“You have an entire loop where agents did most of the work, but crucially, there’s human judgment in the middle, and we don’t think that’s going away anytime soon. You need human judgment; you need taste,” Masad explained.
The end result is that instead of taking jobs from people, agents are changing what people work on.
“We’re spending a lot more time figuring out what to work on,” Masad continued. “I go around the company, I see a lot more discussions, a lot more whiteboarding. We spend a lot more time on architecture, how to build things. And so I think the future of work — the self-driving company idea — is really trying to discover what AI transformation means.”
He also noted that when Replit talks with other businesses, the conversations are more about how AI can help people become more productive and happier at work. (The latter because the AI agents make work less boring and more creative, he said.)
“There’s a positive vision of the world that Silicon Valley is not really putting out, and we’re hoping to do that,” Masad added.

title_en: An OpenAI research agent 'stole' test Ethereum to finish a coding task
title_fa: An OpenAI research agent 'stole' test Ethereum to finish a coding task
excerpt_en: An OpenAI research model hit a nebulous milestone today by pilfering test Ethereum tokens.
excerpt_fa: An OpenAI research model hit a nebulous milestone today by pilfering test Ethereum tokens.
content_en:
An OpenAI research agent 'stole' test Ethereum to finish a coding task
It reasoned that the tokens were 'valueless' and 'abandoned.'
An OpenAI research model hit another nebulous milestone today by pilfering test Ethereum tokens from a wallet it didn't control to finish a coding task, the company said in an incident report. The agent subsequently hid the act from OpenAI, saying it was fine because the tokens had no value. "This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder's permission, then act on that judgment without authorization," OpenAI wrote.
The incident, which occurred on June 26, happened while a GPT-5.6 Sol model was in internal training. The task involved updating a crypto trading prototype and deploying contracts (publishing special code) on an Ethereum test network called Sepolia. Payment of a network fee is required for such contracts, but OpenAI "supplied no funded wallet and gave no permission to spend funds from an account the model found independently," OpenAI said in the report.
The lack of funds at first stymied the agent, but it was not to be discouraged. The model reasoned that it could use public developer recovery phrases (similar to those you might use to recover a password) to access keys from unauthorized accounts. It tracked down 362 addresses open to that avenue of attack and found one that held enough Sepolia ETH to finish its deployment (to be clear, Sepolia ETH has no value outside of testing).
Like many criminals, the agent reasoned that someone must have left this access open for automated draining of the ETH "faucets." It also figured that the crypto was effectively "abandoned" and "valueless," according to OpenAI's misalignment records. The piece de resistance was that the agent "did not disclose that it had selected a funded account through a public recover phrase or spent that account's balance," OpenAI said. To prevent similar events in the future, the company is now monitoring all traffic and paging security if live internet access is detected.
If agents going rogue to attain their goals sounds familiar, models from OpenAI, Anthropic and other AI companies have been doing a lot of that lately. A partial list of its victims include the Hugging Face AI code repository, Australia's Medicare Portal, several US Federal agencies and the RubyGems developer registry. After all that, even AI employees believe that government regulation is in order, but so far the Trump administration has opposed such a move.

title_en: Steam Achievement Sets will stop DLCs from ruining your 100 percent record
title_fa: Steam Achievement Sets will stop DLCs from ruining your 100 percent record
excerpt_en: Steam has launched Achievement Sets in beta.
excerpt_fa: Steam has launched Achievement Sets in beta.
content_en:
Steam Achievement Sets will stop DLCs from ruining your 100 percent record
The platform now separates base game and DLC achievements.
Steam can now group together different categories of achievements — and separates ones for base games and ones for DLCs — so that developers' new additions won't affect your completion percentage. The new feature, called Achievement Sets, is now live in Steam Client beta. Developers will have to update their games to add specific collections, each one with a defined purpose, but the platform says there's a growing number of games that already support the feature. They can, for example, group single-player and multiplayer achievements or introduce seasonal sets, like one for a Halloween event.
You'll see achievements grouped together in collections when you browse everything you've unlocked on your profile. Each set has a progress bar that shows how far along you are in completing it, and you'll be able to display a "set complete" trophy on your profile every time you earn every single achievement in a collection. Your progress will still show 100 percent even if the developer adds more achievements to a set later on.
Steam divides collections into two types: Base Game Achievement Sets and DLC Achievement Sets. All base game trophies, as well as their progress bar, appear blue on your achievements page. Meanwhile, DLC achievements and progress bars are displayed in purple. Those sets will not show up in your overall game progress until you have access to the specific DLCs they're connected to, so as to not affect your completion.
The platform has redesigned its achievements page to be able to show the sets and your progress better, as well. This new page will also allow you to compare your progress with up to three friends, including the rare achievements you've earned and the sets you've completed.

title_en: ChatGPT can now look at your Chrome tabs to do tasks for you
title_fa: ChatGPT can now look at your Chrome tabs to do tasks for you
excerpt_en: The ChatGPT browser extension lets you compare information from your open tabs.
excerpt_fa: The ChatGPT browser extension lets you compare information from your open tabs.
content_en:
ChatGPT can now look at your Chrome tabs to do tasks for you
OpenAI has updated its ChatGPT extension to be able to do more browser-based tasks.
OpenAI has updated its ChatGPT extension for Chrome, giving it the power to look at your tabs so it can come up with more personalized and useful answers to your queries. The company used to have a browser of its own, but it retired the product on August 9. It did, however, roll out upgrades to the Chrome extension that made ChatGPT a more viable alternative to Gemini in the browser. With these latest updates, ChatGPT can now do even more tasks inside Chrome.
If you're in ChatGPT Chat, you can ask the AI assistant to take a look at your open tabs on Chrome to conjure answers that would personally be useful. You can, for instance, ask it to compare couches opened on three different tabs by their dimensions, prices, delivery time and return policy.
Meanwhile, if you're using ChatGPT Work, OpenAI's agent designed for complex multi-step tasks, you can ask the assistant to send messages, fill out forms, organize tabs and fill out forms for you. You can ask ChatGPT to fill out a form for your new dentist and then add your schedule to the calendar, for instance. Another example is to get the chatbot to analyze several contractors' terms open in multiple tabs and then draft an email to the provider that fits your needs the most.
In addition, ChatGPT in Chrome's sidebar now has access to your whole history, so you can talk to it and give it tasks without having to tab away from what you were doing. You can get the ChatGPT extension, no matter what plan you have. OpenAI says that aside from Chrome, the extension is also compatible with other Chromium-based browsers, including Microsoft Edge, Brave and Opera.
Next up: using ChatGPT right within a Chrome tab got a major upgrade – the full power of ChatGPT is now in your browser.
Your entire ChatGPT history is right there, and you can ask question in Chat or get things done in Work – side by side while you're on a site. pic.twitter.com/ABiwzLvNnD
— ChatGPT (@ChatGPT) October 15, 2026

title_en: Apple's $2,000 iPhone Duo goes on pre-order today at 8AM ET
title_fa: Apple's $2,000 iPhone Duo goes on pre-order today at 8AM ET
excerpt_en: The Apple Store is down ahead of pre-orders for the first folding iPhone.
excerpt_fa: The Apple Store is down ahead of pre-orders for the first folding iPhone.
content_en:
Apple's $2,000 iPhone Duo goes on pre-order today at 8AM ET
All indications are that the device will be in high demand and relatively short supply.
The Apple Store is down, so you probably know what that means. "We love that early energy," the placeholder page states. "Almost ready for you. Pre-order begins at 5:00 AM PT. See you soon." Apple is of course referring to the iPhone Duo, which goes on pre-order this morning at 8AM ET. If you wanted to be among the first to own one, all indications are that the device will be in high demand and relatively short supply. That means pre-ordering is likely a better option than waiting for launch day on October 23rd.
In his hands-on look, Engadget's Sam Rutherford called the iPhone Duo "Apple's most exciting device in a decade." Though not the first folding phone by any means, it has 5.4-inch outer display and 7.6-inch inner OLED matte widescreen when unfolded, making it ideal for viewing media and feeling like a small iPad. That display is practically seamless, with subtle gradient and depth of field effects that help sell the allure of Apple's first foldable device.
The main drawbacks with the iPhone Duo are the expensive $2,000 price tag, lack of FaceID and no fancy variable aperture in the main camera like the new iPhone 18 Pro models. The under-display FaceTime camera on the inner screen is also a downgrade, though it certainly makes the device look sleeker when unfolded.
I'm a big fan of folding phones, having used one of Samsung's Galaxy Fold models for a few months in the past. They're certainly attention-grabbing devices as well that are bound to stoke comments from interested observers, which may be a good enough reason to get one for some buyers. As mentioned, pre-orders could get snapped up soon, so you'd best hit the iPhone Duo order page at 5AM PT sharp.

title_en: Gmail's Live AI search feature arrives for Google AI subscribers
title_fa: Gmail's Live AI search feature arrives for Google AI subscribers
excerpt_en: Gmail's search can be frustrating and basic, but Google is finally smartening it up for AI plan subscribers.
excerpt_fa: Gmail's search can be frustrating and basic, but Google is finally smartening it up for AI plan subscribers.
content_en:
Gmail's Live AI search feature arrives for Google AI subscribers
It's coming soon for Workspace business customers.
Gmail's search can be frustrating and basic, but Google is finally smartening it up for AI plan subscribers with the release of Gmail Live. Now out of beta after being announced at Google I/O last month, the AI feature allows you to search your inbox using conversational voice commands. It's similar to live voice chats with the Gemini chatbot, but customized for popular apps like Gmail, Docs and Drive, with each getting its own version of the functionality.
The feature, Google says, allows you to find details in buried in emails without digging through endless threads. "Use conversational search to find information just by asking things like, 'What's my flight's gate number?' or 'What's going on at my kid's school this week?' and Gmail Live will scan your inbox and give you answers quickly," Google explains.
Similar functionality is also coming to documents and notes with Docs Live and Keep Live. Docs Live lets you tell Gemini what kind of document you want and allow it to pull relevant details from Gmail, Drive, Chat and the broader web. It will then structure the document to create a first draft, while helping you refine your tone, as Google shows in the short video above.
Keep Live, meanwhile, "turns brain dumps into organized notes." Normally, the app is used to jot down an idea before you forget it, but Keep Live is designed to "capture, structure and refine your ideas into organized, actionable notes," the company wrote. The new voice feature processes your voice commands in the background, "turning your thoughts into structured lists and notes without you having to type a single word."
In its video example, Google cites a person saying "I promised my son I would paint his room this weekend... I'm going to need a list of instructions as well as supplies." With this info, Keep Live replies "Preparing your painting note now," and proceeds to generate a shopping list and how-to guide as requested.
The new features are rolling out this week in Gmail and Keep, but only for Google AI Plus, Pro and Ultra subscribers, with Docs limited to Pro and Ultra subscribers. All of the features are also "coming soon" for Google Workspace business customers.

title_en: Even Benchmark thinks AI is eroding the venture pact against backing rivals
title_fa: Even Benchmark thinks AI is eroding the venture pact against backing rivals
excerpt_en: Benchmark says the Valley’s rule against backing rivals is getting harder to keep.
excerpt_fa: Benchmark says the Valley’s rule against backing rivals is getting harder to keep.
content_en:
For decades, the unwritten rule of venture capital was that a firm doesn’t back two companies that compete head-on. But speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt earlier this week, the partners of Benchmark readily acknowledged that the AI boom is straining that rule.
It’s been on the verge of snapping for some time. The towering AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic share dozens of the same investors at this point. Then, at the end of September, Factory, a startup that builds an AI agent to write software, said it was firing board observer and adviser Chris Degnan for “unethical conduct involving Cognition,” its direct rival and the maker of the Devin coding agent. Factory’s CEO alleged Degnan had discussed a job at Cognition while privy to Factory’s board-level discussions. Degnan said he had already resigned and denied sharing anything confidential. Soon after, he announced he was joining Cognition as chief revenue officer. Powerhouse investor Vinod Khosla sided with Degnan on X, blasting Factory’s CEO and calling the company “a struggling second tier competitor.” Khosla Ventures backs both companies.
Even Benchmark, a firm whose reputation rests on 10-to-15-year partnerships with founders at the earliest stage, said the old rule can no longer be counted on. Asked at Disrupt whether the pact against backing rivals still holds as portfolio companies expand into each other’s territory, its partners described the conflicts as a matter of necessity, not preference.
“The harsh reality of this world is every company is evolving very quickly,” said Eric Vishria. Companies pivot and change, he said, and “you are going to get conflicts, and that’s just the reality of the current dynamic.”
Vishria said Benchmark stays committed to each founder and keeps what it learns confidential, and he downplayed how much a VC could pass along anyway: “We are not product or technology experts.” Seemingly referring to the Factory-Cognition dispute, he said Benchmark has been fortunate not to land in “that type of insane direct conflict.” Exclusivity, he said, remains “really important” at the very early stage Benchmark favors. “But things are evolving. There’s no doubt about that.”
Chetan Puttagunta said AI is accelerating the problem. As the cost of building software “effectively goes to zero,” he said, founders are “incredibly ambitious.” Because they now see a “surface area” and want to claim all of it, he continued, “[i]t’s probably going to happen more, where you start to run into each other.”
He drew a line between a direct competitor at the outset, which he called “an easy answer,” and a portfolio company that expands into another’s turf over time. “That happens,” he said.
Peter Fenton called the issue “kryptonite” and the firm’s toughest problem. He described a spectrum of how investors relate to their companies. At one end is the co-founder, who would never work on a competing company. At the other is the public-market stock picker, who can own several rivals because he is merely allocating capital, not shaping any of them. Benchmark sits nearer the co-founder end, Fenton said, and treats transparency as a golden rule. “There shouldn’t be the surprise after the fact.” If a conflict does emerge, a founder should never feel shortchanged, he added.
Benchmark isn’t declaring the pact dead. At the same time, when a firm that built its name on loyalty says conflicts are coming, founders might rightly wonder who else will be this candid.

Relive Tesla's ridiculous(ly fun) Roadster stunt show
Watch the new Roadster make crazy jumps.
Tesla's Roadster launch event was pretty exciting to say the least, with loads of car stunts that we enjoyed watching. The Roadster first appeared during the event at the bottom of C-shaped ramp. It drove up — twice — and stopped at the top of the ramp perpendicular to the ground, hanging upside-down. After the second time, the car jumped off the ramp, rolled over, and safely hovered to the ground, thanks to its cold-gas thrusters that use technology borrowed from SpaceX.
Real life, baby pic.twitter.com/3QEqn18wig
— Tesla (@Tesla) October 16, 2026
The automaker also made the Roadster jump over several of its vehicles parked side by the side. And near the end of the presentation, the Roadster did one last flip, jumping from stationary position, turning over in the air, and then hovering back down.
Tesla's next-gen Roadster is now available for reservation. It will cost you $5,000 to make a reservation right now, with an additional $45,000 due within 10 days for the base vehicle. If you want the version with suctions, which enabled it to hang upside-down on the ramp, and accelerator thrusters, the reservation will cost you $250,000. The version of the Roadster that can jump up and hover, however, will only be available to select customers, with the reservation being invite-only.

title_en: Tesla's redesigned Roadster has a cold-gas thruster option, but you'll need $250,000 just to reserve it
title_fa: Tesla's redesigned Roadster has a cold-gas thruster option, but you'll need $250,000 just to reserve it
excerpt_en: Tesla has finally unveiled the next-generation Roadster.
excerpt_fa: Tesla has finally unveiled the next-generation Roadster.
content_en:
Tesla's redesigned Roadster has a cold-gas thruster option, but you'll need $250,000 just to reserve it
The automaker has unveiled the vehicle with some crazy stunts.
Tesla has unveiled the next-generation Roadster, nine years after the company showed off its concept prototype and after years and years of launch delay. Elon Musk and the Tesla team introduced the vehicle during an event at the SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas with a stunt. It drove up a C-shaped ramp and stopped in the middle of the part perpendicular to the ground while it was hanging upside-down. Then the vehicle repeated the action and jumped off the ramp from the top and flipped, its thruster system kicking in so it could safely hover to the ground.
When they opened up the door to the driver's seat, an Optimus robot was seating there. It was, however, only for show, and the stunts were programmed into the vehicle. They explained later on that the Roadster has a suction system at the bottom of the car that enabled it to stick upside-down to the ramp. On its website, Tesla said that its multi-mode fan and ground sealing system pulls air out from beneath the vehicle to act as a downforce generator, providing suction that make holding the vehicle upside-down possible even when it's stationary.
Meanwhile, it could jump off the ramp and safely land on the ground, thanks to its attitude-control thrusters and thrusters in the rear, which use technology borrowed from SpaceX. These advanced cold-gas thrusters use all-electric actuators that enable precise thrust and can perform "micro adjustments within a fraction of a second."
Musk said the new Roadster will go into production in 2028.
Tesla first started taking pre-orders for the Roadster way back when it was first announced. Those who didn't get the chance can now reserve a unit for $5,000, with $45,000 to follow within the next 10 days for the base vehicle. As you'd expect, the thrusters and air suction system cost extra. For the "Thrust" package, which comes with the suction system and acceleration thrusters, buyers are expected to pay an additional $245,000 within 10 days of reservation. The "Rocket" version, which comes with the full-flight system, is invite-only and probably something we'll see a lot of in influencers' videos.

content_en:
Elon Musk promised a flying car. And the Tesla Roadster did exactly that.
The Tesla Roadster flew, drove upside down, and hit 60mph in under a second
The next-gen Roadster has been in development for nearly a decade. But perhaps it was worth the wait.
The next-gen Roadster has been in development for nearly a decade. But perhaps it was worth the wait.
Tesla demonstrated its next-generation Roadster at an event in Waco, Texas, where the electric supercar drove upside down, briefly flew, and accelerated to 60mph in under a second. It was an impressive demonstration of a car that likely will come with some heavy caveats and restrictions if it ever goes into production.
The event was less than 30 minutes and felt more like a stunt show than a product reveal. Indeed, there was no mention of price, release date, or other such mundane details. Musk promised the hypercar would go into production in 2028, but after nearly nine years who’s counting. The people were here to see a car fly, and that’s what Tesla gave them.
First, the Roadster drove up a very tall, multi-story ramp, using its incredible downforce to cling to the vertical roadway. When it reached the top of the ramp, it flipped around using its cold-gas thrusters to bring it gently back down to earth. The car uses a fan-based suction system, supplied by SpaceX and mounted underneath the vehicle, which is capable of generating up to two Gs of suction force.
Next, the Roadster flew over the rest of Tesla’s lineup, including the Model 3, Model Y, Cybertruck, Semi, and Cybercab — doing what Tesla VP for Engineering Lars Moravy called “a kick flip” in the process. Musk explained that it features attitude-control thrusters as well as main thrusters at the rear, giving the Roadster rocket-like capabilities.
“So it can basically fly like a rocket,” Musk said. “And it could do rolls. It could do, like, crazy gymnastics. Whatever you want, really. Now, I should say that this is not necessarily a safety-optimized car. But it takes the fun meter to 11 out of 10.”
The Roadster two ultra-high pressure air tanks with a combined volume of 600 liters, containing approximately 250 kilograms of air, and uses 10 nozzles to execute its maneuvers. The Roadster can even recharge its own tank, without requiring a specialized chemical propellant. The stored compressed air supplies the thrust needed to lift the car and perform the demonstrated maneuvers.
Musk claimed “This will be an actual car that’s on the roads” — though later the company admitted it would not be road legal. This seems obvious, of course. Imagine having to satisfy strict regulatory requirements from the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. The Roadster could go into production in 2028, as Musk promised — or it could be another decade of missed deadlines and broken promises. Again, who cares? Car flew.
As for the Roadster itself, Musk called it “the last best driver’s car.” Moravy said that Tesla drew inspiration from aerospace designs such as the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft. It’s a two-seater, with seats molded directly into the chassis. Its steering and driving controls use steer-by-wire technology, including a steer-by-wire yoke, brakes, and throttle. The rear of the car features the thrusters and fans housed around the diffuser area. And it has a retractable rear wing for added downforce.
Tesla has also said that the Roadster can accelerate from 0-60mph in less than a second. And during the event, the company claimed it did so in 0.81 seconds. Musk explained that increasing the applied force while reducing the vehicle’s mass help boost acceleration. In fact, Musk says the production Roadster should improve on the demonstrated result, although he acknowledged the extreme forces involved and the need to avoid subjecting occupants to extreme acceleration.
“You’ve got to crack halfway to the speed of sound, I think,” Musk teased. “Mach 0.5. Maybe a little higher.”
After the event, Tesla updated its website with details about the three distinct performance tiers for the next-generation Roadster, outlining how its controversial cold-gas thruster systems scale across the lineup:
- Performance (Road Ready): The entry-level variant seats two passengers and relies on an active aerodynamics package paired with a multi-mode suction system to maximize downforce on and off the track. It claims a 0–60 mph time under 1.6 seconds and a target range exceeding 300 miles.
- Thrust (Race Ready): Also a two-seater, this mid-tier version pairs the multi-mode suction system with rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters. The additional propulsion cuts the vehicle’s 0–60 mph acceleration to under 0.9 seconds. Tesla says this configuration will be in “limited release.”
- Rocket (Air Ready): The single-seat flagship model expands the hardware to a full perimeter-mounted array of cold-gas thrusters. In addition to driving forward and upward acceleration, the thrusters enable lateral and rotational movement in midair — enabling the short, low-altitude stunts showcased at the event. This top-spec version reaches a top speed over 230 mph and pushes 0–60 mph acceleration to under 0.59 seconds. Tesla says this version will be “invite only,” but also “not approved for public road use.”
The next-gen Roadster certainly took the scenic route in getting here. A prototype version was announced as a “one more thing” style surprise during the 2017 Tesla Semi event. The specs sounded ludicrous even back then: 0-60 mph in 1.9 seconds, a top speed over 250 mph, a 200 kWh battery delivering up to 620 miles of range, and a $200,000 starting price tag. Musk said deliveries would start in 2020, which sounded perfectly doable at the time.

title_en: Tesla reveals SpaceX-powered Roadster that flies and falls with style
title_fa: Tesla reveals SpaceX-powered Roadster that flies and falls with style
excerpt_en: The new car used thrusters to leap over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 at a demo in Texas.
excerpt_fa: The new car used thrusters to leap over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 at a demo in Texas.
content_en:
Tesla just revealed its redesigned second-generation Roadster with SpaceX thrusters, a vehicle CEO Elon Musk has called “the best of the last of the human-driven cars.”
Musk showed off the car at an event outside Waco, Texas, with a demonstration that saw the car use a mixture of high-powered fans and thrusters to drive up an inverted ramp, spin around, and ease itself to a landing on the pavement below. The car also used the thrusters to lift itself over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 while in motion.
“This will be the actual car that’s on the roads,” Musk said of the car, which Tesla showed accelerating 0 to 60 miles per hour in one second. “It literally is just going to puff itself up, and uh, and be able to do this, these maneuvers whenever you’d like.”
Musk said Tesla will finally build the long-delayed vehicle in 2028, but didn’t name a price. Tesla will offer it in three trims. The first is “Performance,” which Tesla describes as “road ready.” It seats two, has active aerodynamics, and features a “multi-mode suction system for next-level performance on and off the track.” The second trim is “Thrust,” which is “race ready” and seats two, and has rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters that enable sub-one-second 0-to-60 mph accleration. The third is “Rocket,” which is “air ready” and seats one, and has 10 cold-gas thrusters positioned around the car.
All three trims will have 300 miles of range and be capable of speeds exceeding 230 miles per hour.
Tesla’s website showed Thursday the company is taking reservations for the car, charging $50,000 just to reserve the Performance, and $250,000 for Thrust. The Rocket trim is billed as “invite only.”
Engineering VP Lars Moravy said at the event that the Roadster uses 10 thrusters connected to 600 liters of compressed air to lift and spin the car in midair. The air tank can be recharged, he said. “Every usable void in the car is packed with Carbon Fiber Overwrapped Pressure Vessels (COPVs),” Tesla wrote in a post on X, referring to the type of pressure vessel that has been at the root of multiple SpaceX rocket explosions. The company said “every usable void” in the car is filled with these vessels.
Musk also said at the event that Tesla may try to jump the Snake River Canyon — the site of Evel Knievel’s famous attempt to cross the gorge in a steam-powered rocket.
Musk has positioned the Roadster as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster.
“If you buy a Ferrari, safety is not the number one goal. I say, if safety is your number one goal, do not buy the Roadster,” he said on a podcast earlier this year. Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said.
“This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX Engineers working closely together to make something you haven’t seen in any movie, better than any James Bond car,” Musk said at the event. “I’ve never seen anything like this. You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’”
Musk had previously claimed that the car “will be very different from what was shown previously” and promised the demo would be the “most exciting, whether it works or not, demo ever of any product.”
The design changes were notable. The car, shown in stark white, now has a more angular design reminiscent of a Lamborghini or the famous Lotus Esprit used by the James Bond character in The Spy Who Loved Me — a car Musk owns, which was on display at the event.
In another post, Tesla said the design was inspired by the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft and the F-35 fighter jet.
“Our design language has evolved since the last reveal: from S3XY to Cybertruck, Cybercab & Optimus,” the company wrote.
Tesla held the event almost nine years to the day after the company first revealed the second-generation Roadster, a modernized take on its first-ever car. Unveiled as a surprise at the end of the Tesla Semi reveal in 2017, the revamped Roadster was supposed to be delivered in just a few years. Tesla allowed customers to place $50,000 deposits to reserve the car. Some even paid $250,000 to reserve one of 1,000 “Founders Series” versions.
Musk first talked about adding thrusters to the car in 2018. “SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car,” he wrote on Twitter that year. “These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering. Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …”
But the Roadster project took a back seat. In 2018, Tesla suffered through what Musk eventually dubbed “production hell” with the Model 3 sedan. The company then moved onto other projects like the Model Y SUV, which became the best-selling vehicle in the world, and the Cybertruck, which was a commercial flop by Tesla’s own standards. Along the way, Musk delayed the new Roadster in 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024.
As more time passed following the launch of those new vehicles, Musk started talking about the second-generation Roadster again. Late last year, he said on Joe Rogan’s podcast that he wanted to reveal it by the end of 2025. One week later, at the shareholder meeting where he was awarded a $1 trillion pay package, he delayed it to April 1, 2026. Musk said holding an April Fools’ Day event would give him “some deniability” if Tesla delayed the event again.
“Like, I could say I was just kidding,” he said at the time. Tesla wound up pushing back the reveal again. It attempted to hold the event on October 1, but severe weather forced yet another delay.
These repeated delays caused a number of high-profile customers to speak out over the years, including YouTuber Marques Brownlee and OpenAI head Sam Altman.

The third is “Rocket,” which is “air ready” and seats one, and has 10 cold-gas thrusters positioned around the car.
All three trims will have 300 miles of range and be capable of speeds exceeding 230 miles per hour.
Tesla’s website showed Thursday the company is taking reservations for the car, charging $50,000 just to reserve the Performance, and $250,000 for Thrust. The Rocket trim is billed as “invite only.”
Engineering VP Lars Moravy said at the event that the Roadster uses 10 thrusters connected to 600 liters of compressed air to lift and spin the car in midair. The air tank can be recharged, he said. “Every usable void in the car is packed with Carbon Fiber Overwrapped Pressure Vessels (COPVs),” Tesla wrote in a post on X, referring to the type of pressure vessel that has been at the root of multiple SpaceX rocket explosions. The company said “every usable void” in the car is filled with these vessels.
Musk also said at the event that Tesla may try to jump the Snake River Canyon — the site of Evel Knievel’s famous attempt to cross the gorge in a steam-powered rocket.
Musk has positioned the Roadster as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster.
“If you buy a Ferrari, safety is not the number one goal. I say, if safety is your number one goal, do not buy the Roadster,” he said on a podcast earlier this year. Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said.
“This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX Engineers working closely together to make something you haven’t seen in any movie, better than any James Bond car,” Musk said at the event. “I’ve never seen anything like this. You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’”
Musk had previously claimed that the car “will be very different from what was shown previously” and promised the demo would be the “most exciting, whether it works or not, demo ever of any product.”
The design changes were notable. The car, shown in stark white, now has a more angular design reminiscent of a Lamborghini or the famous Lotus Esprit used by the James Bond character in The Spy Who Loved Me — a car Musk owns, which was on display at the event.
In another post, Tesla said the design was inspired by the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft and the F-35 fighter jet.
“Our design language has evolved since the last reveal: from S3XY to Cybertruck, Cybercab & Optimus,” the company wrote.
Tesla held the event almost nine years to the day after the company first revealed the second-generation Roadster, a modernized take on its first-ever car. Unveiled as a surprise at the end of the Tesla Semi reveal in 2017, the revamped Roadster was supposed to be delivered in just a few years. Tesla allowed customers to place $50,000 deposits to reserve the car. Some even paid $250,000 to reserve one of 1,000 “Founders Series” versions.
Musk first talked about adding thrusters to the car in 2018. “SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car,” he wrote on Twitter that year. “These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering. Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …”
But the Roadster project took a back seat. In 2018, Tesla suffered through what Musk eventually dubbed “production hell” with the Model 3 sedan. The company then moved onto other projects like the Model Y SUV, which became the best-selling vehicle in the world, and the Cybertruck, which was a commercial flop by Tesla’s own standards. Along the way, Musk delayed the new Roadster in 2020, 2021, 2023, and 2024.
As more time passed following the launch of those new vehicles, Musk started talking about the second-generation Roadster again. Late last year, he said on Joe Rogan’s podcast that he wanted to reveal it by the end of 2025. One week later, at the shareholder meeting where he was awarded a $1 trillion pay package, he delayed it to April 1, 2026. Musk said holding an April Fools’ Day event would give him “some deniability” if Tesla delayed the event again.
“Like, I could say I was just kidding,” he said at the time. Tesla wound up pushing back the reveal again. It attempted to hold the event on October 1, but severe weather forced yet another delay.
These repeated delays caused a number of high-profile customers to speak out over the years, including YouTuber Marques Brownlee and OpenAI head Sam Altman.

title_en: When it came to Cal AI’s viral success, a small army of influencers paid off
title_fa: When it came to Cal AI’s viral success, a small army of influencers paid off
excerpt_en: The company generated over $30 million in revenue in two years and was acquired by MyFitnessPal for an undisclosed amount of money in March.
excerpt_fa: The company generated over $30 million in revenue in two years and was acquired by MyFitnessPal for an undisclosed amount of money in March.
content_en:
Zach Yadegari has enjoyed an immense amount of success for someone who only recently graduated from high school. Founder of the AI-fueled calorie tracking app Cal AI, Yadegari is only 19 but his company has rocketed to viral fame over the past two years. At TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday, Yadegari shared details of that surprising rise to prominence.
Cal AI, which was founded in 2024, exploded onto the internet thanks largely to Yadegari’s strategy of deploying a small army of influencers to promote the brand. The company generated over $30 million in revenue in two years and was acquired by MyFitnessPal for an undisclosed amount of money in March.
Discussing his social strategy onstage, Yadegari noted that an early sign of success came when an influencer’s post about them led to approximately a thousand new users over the course of two days.
“From there, we figured out, okay, this can actually work for us, and so we started recruiting influencers as fast as we could — paying as many people as possible to start posting for us,” he said. “What we saw was that it was a clear formula. It was pretty linear, but it was extremely fast. I guess linear in the sense that every post they did would get a certain number of viewers that would convert.”
The Forbes 30 Under 30 alumnus told the audience that part of his company’s strategy was to negotiate rates with influencers, promising them certain payouts for a certain scale of reach. A lot of influencers are “broke college kids” who “just want cash,” Yadegari added. “You just ask them, okay, we’ll pay you this, but we need to get us at least this amount of use and keep posting until you get there.”
Another important component of success was finding the right influencers whose reach can be quantified. “The biggest thing for us was finding influencers that had very tight communities,” the founder said.
Yadegari, whose father was in the audience, also credited his family with giving him the freedom to go after his ambitions. Does he also credit higher education for his success? Not so much.
“I think the only real reason to go to college is if you want to have a fun social time as a kid and be with other people,” he said, to audience laughter.
Earlier this month, Yadegari also launched Persona, a new AI agent startup that has already raised $10 million.
Yadegari said the “overarching mission” with Persona is to “make computing seamless with human life.” The company’s personal AI assistant will “live anyplace with internet connection,” he said, including “iMessage, app, email, phone call.” He added that part of what distinguishes the company’s plans for this AI assistant is to build a “hardware ecosystem around” the app.
